title: Playing in all keys and the keys used in jazz
summary: He admits he could not play in all keys and says jazz stayed in C, F, B flat, E flat and A flat because few players handled sharps.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Could you play in any key?
I'll have to admit, no, I couldn't play in all keys so well.
No. You know, there's -- in fact I think you could live all your life, and I don't think there's very many people who can play in all keys as well as they can play in others.
This is one of the things we practiced, you know, playing in other keys. But at that time, you know, the jazz music was played in the key of C, F, B flat, E flat, and A flat.
But you sort of stayed away from those sharps.
Because you couldn't get that many people to play in those keys, so you couldn't get to practice if you played in those keys.

You couldn't play with anybody because they couldn't play in those keys. Then there are some keys that are just not practical, just like life. You know, there's such a thing as making something too complicated, you know.
When it's too complicated it's no good.
No. And the key that might, you know, might possibly work out for you, is not going to be a good key for the alto or the tenor saxophone player, or even the (inaudible)
And so on, because they're going to be in a different key too.
That's right. But as I said, as you get more proficient, and you get more experience, you learn to play in all keys, and be simple.
